_source: Helen Edgar's Myths & Legends, behind her Faery Yurt through the Alchemist's Arch, asked for on 2026-10-25: more faery and myth, The Golden Bough, English folklore, King Arthur and Merlin, and Stonehenge made more magical. Every fact here was read on the page its source names, on the day in _checked, and the words are ours, never copied: English Heritage for the stones, the British Library and the old texts on Project Gutenberg where they say it, Aberystwyth University and Nature for the Altar Stone, and Wikipedia for the rest. Where sources disagree the wording says so or takes the safer figure. Edit this, then run tools/make-yurt-myths.py, which writes it into faery-myths-room.html and refuses a fact with no source.

summer.says: At midsummer, standing in the middle of the circle, you see the sun rise just to the left of the Heel Stone, the big stone outside the circle, along the line of the Avenue.

winter.says: At midwinter, looking the other way, the sun would once have set between the two uprights of the tallest trilithon. Half of that trilithon has fallen, so the view is gone, but the line is still the same.

facts.says: It was built in stages: first a round ditch with banks inside and out, about 3000 BC, and the great stones put up about 2500 BC.
Most of the big sarsen stones came from West Woods, on the Marlborough Downs, about 15 miles to the north. That was found in 2020 by matching their chemistry.
The smaller bluestones came about 150 miles, from the Preseli Hills in south-west Wales.
The Altar Stone came further still: in 2024 it was traced to north-east Scotland, at least 700 km (about 435 miles) away.
facts.source_name: Aberystwyth University, on Clarke et al. in Nature, 2024

facts.says: The druids did not build it. It is more than 2,000 years older than anything written about druids. John Aubrey in the 1600s and William Stukeley in the 1700s were the ones who linked it to them.
On the summer solstice English Heritage lets everybody in to the stones for free, and streams the sunset and the sunrise online.

nearby.name: Avebury
nearby.says: The largest stone circle in Britain, with a village built partly inside it.

nearby.name: Silbury Hill
nearby.says: The largest artificial mound in Europe, probably finished around 2400 BC, and nobody is sure what it was for.

nearby.name: Wayland's Smithy
nearby.says: A Neolithic long barrow, a tomb older than Stonehenge's stones. The story, written down in 1738, is that if you left your horse there with a coin, you came back to find the coin gone and the horse new shod, by Wayland the smith.

nearby.name: The Uffington White Horse
nearby.says: A horse cut into the chalk hillside about 3,000 years ago, in the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age.

layers.says: The Historia Brittonum, a history of the Britons traditionally said to be by Nennius, lists twelve battles fought by Arthur, the last on Mount Badon.
The Welsh Annals give one line to Camlann, the strife “in which Arthur and Medraut fell”.

Geoffrey of Monmouth writes the first full life of Arthur: Uther Pendragon, Arthur's birth at Tintagel, Merlin, the last battle, and Arthur carried away to the isle of Avalon. Most of it seems to be his own invention.
In France, Chrétien de Troyes brings in Lancelot, and is the first writer to tell of the Holy Grail.
William Caxton prints Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the great English telling that most later versions grow from.
Most historians do not think Arthur was a real person; he is a figure of story and folklore, and a very long-lived one.

people.name: Merlin
people.says: The enchanter, who in Geoffrey's story brings the stones of Stonehenge over from Ireland, and arranges Arthur's birth.
people.source_name: Geoffrey of Monmouth, in Giles's Old English Chronicles

people.name: The Lady of the Lake
people.says: In Malory an arm clothed in white samite rises from the lake holding Excalibur. Malory has two swords: the one Arthur pulls from the stone, which breaks in a fight, and Excalibur from the lake. (He calls Arthur's sword Excalibur once before the lake too.)
people.source_name: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I

people.name: Nimue
people.says: A lady of the lake whom Merlin falls for, and who shuts him under a great stone from which he never comes out. Malory gave her the name Nimue; the French romances called her Viviane.

people.name: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
people.says: A late-1300s poem by an unknown writer: a green giant walks into Camelot at Christmas and asks for a beheading game. It survives in only one manuscript, now in the British Library.

places.name: Tintagel
places.says: Geoffrey set Arthur's birth here. In the 1230s Richard, Earl of Cornwall built a castle on the island, very likely to make Geoffrey's scene real.

places.name: Glastonbury
places.says: After a great fire at the abbey in 1184, the monks said in 1191 that they had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere. Historians mostly see it as a way of raising money.

places.name: Cadbury Castle
places.says: A great hill fort, lived in from the Neolithic to the Iron Age, that John Leland wrote down in 1542 as Camelot, from what local people said.

places.name: The Round Table
places.says: A real round table hangs on the wall, but tree rings date it to the late 1200s, probably made for Edward I. Henry VIII had it painted as it is now.

creatures.name: Puck, or Robin Goodfellow
creatures.says: A mischief-making household spirit who leads travellers astray and cards the wool while people sleep. Shakespeare put him in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

creatures.name: Boggarts
creatures.says: Spirits that can be a helpful house spirit gone sour, or something lurking in a field, a marsh or a lane. One old Lancashire belief: never give a boggart a name, or it can no longer be reasoned with.

creatures.name: Hobs
creatures.where: northern England, the Midlands and the Borders
creatures.says: Small hairy helpers who do the farm's work at night. One lived in Hob Hole at Runswick Bay in North Yorkshire.

creatures.name: Brownies
creatures.where: Scotland and the north of England
creatures.says: Household spirits who work in the house while everybody sleeps, and vanish for good if you give them clothes.

creatures.name: Black Shuck
creatures.where: Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex and the Fens
creatures.says: A great black ghost dog with burning eyes. On 4 August 1577, in a storm, a black dog was said to have burst into the churches at Bungay and Blythburgh; the door at Blythburgh still has scorch marks people call the devil's fingerprints.

creatures.name: The Lambton Worm
creatures.says: John Lambton, heir to the estate, fished a small worm out of the river and threw it down a well. It grew into a monster that wrapped itself round a hill, and he came home from the Crusades to kill it, and brought a curse on his family.

creatures.name: Herne the Hunter
creatures.says: A ghostly huntsman with antlers who walks round an old oak in Windsor Forest. The first written telling is in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor.

creatures.name: The Green Man
creatures.where: carved in churches all over England
creatures.says: A face made of leaves, or with leaves growing from its mouth, carved in churches mostly from the 1200s to the 1400s. The name was given by Lady Raglan in 1939; what the carvings meant is still argued about.

creatures.name: Will-o'-the-wisp
creatures.says: A strange light over the marsh at night that leads travellers off the path. It has many names: jack-o'-lantern, friar's lantern, hobby lantern and hinkypunk.

creatures.name: Pixies
creatures.where: Devon and Cornwall, on the moors
creatures.says: Small folk of Dartmoor and the West Country. If they lead you round in circles you are pixy-led, and the old answer is to turn your coat inside out.

creatures.name: Knockers
creatures.says: Little people underground who knock on the rock, to warn of a fall or to show the miners where the tin is.

creatures.name: Jenny Greenteeth
creatures.says: A river hag hiding under the green weed on a pond, told of to keep children back from the water. Round Liverpool her name is also a word for duckweed.

creatures.name: The Wild Hunt
creatures.where: the sky on stormy nights, all over Europe
creatures.says: Phantom huntsmen and hounds riding through the sky. In England they were seen in 1127, written down in the Peterborough Chronicle, and Devon has its own Wisht Hounds.

creatures.name: Tom Tit Tot
creatures.says: A small little black thing with a long tail who spins five skeins a day for a girl, and will have her for himself unless she can guess his name: England's own Rumpelstiltskin, first in Joseph Jacobs' English Fairy Tales.

cards.story: Merlin brought the stones of Stonehenge over from Ireland.
cards.fact: That is Geoffrey of Monmouth's story, written in the 1130s. But stones really did travel a long way: the bluestones about 150 miles from Wales, and the Altar Stone more than 400 miles from Scotland.
No. It is more than 2,000 years older than any written mention of druids. The idea comes from John Aubrey and William Stukeley, in the 1600s and 1700s.

cards.story: King Arthur's Round Table hangs in Winchester.
cards.fact: A round table hangs there, but tree rings date it to the late 1200s, hundreds of years after any Arthur could have lived.

cards.story: Arthur and Guinevere are buried at Glastonbury.
cards.fact: The monks said they found the grave in 1191, seven years after a fire had burnt their abbey and they needed money to rebuild. Most historians think that was the point.

cards.story: The Green Man is an ancient pagan god hidden in Christian churches.
cards.fact: The carvings are real and lovely, but the name and the pagan god idea came from Lady Raglan in 1939, and the evidence for it has since been taken apart.

cards.story: Black Shuck burst into Bungay church in 1577.
cards.fact: A pamphlet of 1577 does tell of a black dog in the storm at Bungay. The name Black Shuck is not in it; it was first printed in 1850.

cards.story: Amethyst keeps you from getting drunk.
cards.fact: That is where its name comes from: Greek amethystos means “not drunken”, and people really did believe it. It does not work.

cards.story: Amber is the tears of the sun's daughters.
cards.fact: In Ovid, Phaethon's sisters weep until they turn into trees, and amber drips from the branches and hardens in the sun. Amber is really fossilised tree resin, sometimes with tiny insects caught inside it, so the story was nearly right about the trees.
cards.source_name: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book II, in Riley's translation

wheel.note: Eight festivals round the year: four old Gaelic ones on the quarter days between, and the two solstices and two equinoxes. They are old, but gathering all eight into one wheel is modern, from Gerald Gardner and Ross Nichols in the 1950s and 60s, and the names Litha, Ostara and Mabon were given by Aidan Kelly in the early 1970s.

festivals.name: Samhain
festivals.says: Summer's end, when the old stories say the door to the other world stands open.

festivals.name: Yule
festivals.says: The longest night, and the sun's turn back towards spring.

festivals.name: Imbolc
festivals.says: The coming of spring, and the ewes in lamb.

festivals.name: Ostara
festivals.says: Day and night of equal length.

festivals.name: Beltane
festivals.says: May Day and the start of summer, with bonfires.

festivals.name: Litha, or Midsummer
festivals.says: The longest day, and the sunrise over the Heel Stone.

festivals.name: Lughnasadh, or Lammas
festivals.says: The start of the harvest. In England it was Lammas.

festivals.name: Mabon
festivals.says: Day and night equal again, and the harvest in.

books.title: The Golden Bough
books.says: An enormous gathering of magic, ritual and myth from all over the world, starting from a sacred grove in Italy where a priest-king guarded a golden bough.
books.care: A famous and fascinating book, but Frazer's big theories, of a dying and rising god behind every myth, are now largely set aside by scholars. Read it as an old book, not as fact.

books.title: English Fairy Tales
books.says: Tom Tit Tot, Jack and the Beanstalk, Mr Fox and the rest, gathered from all over England.

books.title: The Fairy Mythology
books.says: Fairies, elves and dwarfs across Europe and beyond, with a long chapter on England's.

books.title: British Goblins
books.says: Welsh fairies, ghosts and spirits, written by an American journalist living in Cardiff.

books.title: The Secret Commonwealth
books.by: Robert Kirk, edited by Andrew Lang
books.says: A Scottish minister's book of the fairies who live in the hills: the Rev. Robert Kirk of Aberfoyle, a seventh son.

books.title: Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry
books.says: The trooping fairies, the solitary fairies, changelings, the banshee and the pooka, gathered by Yeats.

books.title: Le Morte d'Arthur
books.says: The whole story of Arthur in English, from the sword in the stone to Avalon.

books.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
books.says: The Green Knight's Christmas game, told in modern prose.

books.title: Idylls of the King
books.says: Arthur, Guinevere, Lancelot and the Lady of Shalott's Camelot, told by a Victorian poet.

books.title: The History of the Kings of Britain
books.translator: Aaron Thompson, revised by J. A. Giles
books.says: Where Merlin and Arthur's life story first appear, and where Merlin brings the Giants' Dance from Ireland. In Giles's Old English Chronicles.

books.title: The Mabinogion
books.by: Welsh tales of the Middle Ages
books.says: The great Welsh stories, with some of the oldest tales of Arthur in them.

crystals.note: Every stone below is a real one, photographed by somebody who shared the picture, and every meaning is an old belief or a story people tell, not medicine.
crystals.note_says: There is no peer-reviewed scientific evidence that crystal healing has any effect

stones.name: Amethyst
stones.shows: A cluster of purple amethyst crystals from Uruguay, on white.

facts.says: A violet variety of quartz, coloured by iron impurities and natural irradiation.
Big producers include Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul), Artigas in Uruguay, Zambia and Thunder Bay, Ontario.
Heated, amethyst turns yellow-orange or brown and can pass for citrine.

lore.says: Its Greek name, amethystos, means not drunken: people believed it kept the wearer sober, clear-headed and quick-witted.

stones.name: Citrine
stones.shows: A faceted golden-yellow citrine from Brazil, on a warm ground.

facts.says: A transparent yellow variety of quartz; the name comes from citrus, by way of French citron (lemon).
Natural citrine is rare: most 'citrine' sold is heated amethyst or smoky quartz.
Most citrine, natural or heated, comes from Brazil.

lore.says: People believed citrine could soothe tempers and calm the wearer; it has also been called the 'merchant's stone' or 'money stone' from a superstition that it brought prosperity.

stones.name: Garnet
stones.shows: A red-brown garnet crystal sitting on rock.

facts.says: Not one mineral but a group of silicate minerals (almandine, pyrope, spessartine, grossular, andradite, uvarovite).
Used since the Bronze Age as gemstones and abrasives.
The name likely comes from Latin granatum, pomegranate, whose red seeds look like garnet crystals.

lore.says: Some believe garnet brings the wearer good health, wealth and happiness.

stones.name: Moonstone
stones.shows: A pale moonstone crystal from Switzerland, with a soft blue sheen, on black.

facts.says: A feldspar whose milky blue glow (adularescence) comes from light scattered by thin alternating layers of orthoclase and albite.
The commonest moonstone is adularia, named for Mt Adular in Switzerland, where this specimen comes from.
Most commercial moonstone today comes from Sri Lanka; the most valuable blue ones historically came from Myanmar.

lore.says: The Romans believed it was made of solidified rays of the Moon; Hindu mythology says solidified moonbeams, and it was linked with Roman and Greek lunar deities.

stones.name: Labradorite
stones.shows: A polished piece of labradorite from Madagascar, flashing blue, on black.

facts.says: A calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar, first identified in Labrador, Canada (type area Paul's Island near Nain).
Its play of colour is called labradorescence, from very thin layers that form only when the rock cools very slowly.
Spectrolite is a richly coloured kind found at Ylämaa, Finland, in 1940 while fortifications were being built.

lore.says: A story told in Nunatsiavut, on the Labrador coast: an angakok trapped the northern lights in the rocks, and a hunter's harpoon set some of them free. The colours left behind in the stone are labradorite. Told by Jason Sikoak.

stones.name: Lapis lazuli
stones.shows: Deep blue lapis lazuli flecked with gold-coloured pyrite, from Afghanistan.

facts.says: A rock, not a single mineral: mostly lazurite, with pyrite, diopside and calcite.
Mined at Sar-i Sang in Badakhshan, Afghanistan, for more than 6,000 years.
Ground into ultramarine, the blue Renaissance painters such as Titian and Vermeer used.

lore.says: In Mesopotamia it became the chief material for magic stones; it was used in Tutankhamun's funeral mask.

stones.name: Turquoise
stones.shows: A round, knobbly nodule of sky-blue turquoise from Arizona, on white.

facts.says: A blue-to-green hydrous phosphate of copper and aluminium; copper gives the blue.
The name is Old French for 'Turkish': it reached Europe through the Ottoman Empire, though it came from Persia.
It almost never forms single crystals; it fills veins and nodules in rock.

lore.says: From the 1200s it was believed to keep the wearer from falling, especially off a horse. In Tibet it is believed to bring good fortune and protection.

stones.name: Rose quartz
stones.shows: A rough lump of pale pink rose quartz, on white.

facts.says: A pink, translucent variety of quartz that grows as masses, never as well-formed crystals.
Its pink comes from microscopic fibres of a silicate related to dumortierite; it used to be blamed on rutile.
It formed at 400-700 °C in the quartz cores of pegmatites.

lore.says: No older tradition about it was found. Crystal sellers today call it the stone of love.

stones.name: Clear quartz
stones.shows: A cluster of clear quartz points from Brazil, on black.

facts.says: Pure quartz, traditionally called rock crystal or clear quartz, is colourless silicon dioxide.
Quartz is the second most common mineral in the Earth's crust, about 12% by mass.
A quartz crystal keeps time in quartz clocks and watches (the crystal oscillator, 1920s).

lore.says: The Greeks called it krustallos, from kruos 'icy cold': some believed it was supercooled ice, and Pliny the Elder thought it was ice frozen for ages. The idea lasted until the 17th century.

stones.name: Smoky quartz
stones.shows: A tall brown smoky quartz crystal on its rock, from New Mexico, on white.

facts.says: Brown to black quartz, coloured when natural gamma radiation from surrounding rock activates aluminium colour centres.
Cairngorm is a smoky quartz from the Cairngorm Mountains of Scotland, used in Scottish jewellery and kilt pins.
Flat panes of smoky quartz were used as sunglasses in 12th-century China.

lore.says: It was not important in older tradition. Crystal sellers today call it a stone for grounding and cleansing.

stones.name: Obsidian
stones.shows: A glossy black piece of obsidian from Lipari in Sicily, on grey.

facts.says: Volcanic glass, formed when silica-rich lava cools too fast for crystals to grow.
Not a true mineral, because a glass is not crystalline; sometimes called a mineraloid.
It breaks to edges sharper than steel scalpels; Lipari, where this piece comes from, was a Neolithic source of obsidian blades traded widely.

lore.says: Some Aztec priests used obsidian mirrors to conjure visions and make prophecies; they were linked with Tezcatlipoca, 'Smoking Mirror'.

stones.name: Tiger's eye
stones.shows: A rough and a polished piece of tiger's eye, banded gold and brown, reflected in the surface they stand on.

facts.says: Quartz grown in parallel with altered amphibole fibres, mostly turned to limonite; that gives the silky shifting band (chatoyancy).
It forms by the alteration of crocidolite; sources include South Africa, Australia, India, Namibia and Brazil.
Usually cut as a cabochon (a smooth dome) to show the shifting light.

lore.says: In some parts of the world it is believed to ward off the evil eye.

green_shelf._source: Helen Edgar's ask, 2026-10-26: link The Green Witch and The Green Witch's Book of Seasons, and similar books, straight to the publisher and never to Amazon. Both are in Arin Murphy-Hiscock's Green Witch Witchcraft Series (Adams Media, Simon & Schuster), so the shelf is that series. Every title, subtitle and UK publication date was read off its own page at simonandschuster.co.uk on 2026-10-26.
